topic.name: Topic Sentence
topic.job: States the paragraph's argument, answers the essay's directive verb, and frames the counterpoint the paragraph will later evaluate.

criteria.a: Takes a position that answers the directive verb, using explicit evaluative language of degree about the strategy or impact (for example 'highly effective', 'significant', 'limited success'). Saying what was done ('has used X to promote Y', 'has affected Y') without saying how well is description and FAILS, even if a counterpoint follows.
criteria.b: Names BOTH the strategy or policy AND the outcome it influences (for example growth, poverty, development).
criteria.c: Frames the counterpoint: a concessive clause or equivalent qualification (while, although, despite, 'but ... limited by') that signals the limitation.

mechanism.name: Theoretical Mechanism
mechanism.job: Explains step by step how and why the strategy produces the outcome, as economic theory.

criteria.a: The chain is complete and in order: every REQUIRED link listed in the marking notes is present (in any wording). Optional steps may be left out without penalty.
criteria.b: States the economic reason for at least TWO of the key reasons listed in the marking notes (in any wording). FAILS when the links are only asserted with connectors ('consequently X increased') without those reasons. A skipped step belongs to (a), not (b).
criteria.c: Names the economic model or relationship where it fits (AD/AS, AD = C + I + G + (X - M), comparative advantage) and stays on theory. FAILS if the text contains any statistic (a number of people, a percentage, a dollar value, a result tied to a year) or any evaluation of limitations ('although', 'however', 'but' introducing a drawback). The reason must quote any such statistic or drawback, or say 'none found'.

evidence.name: Evidence & Application
evidence.job: Supports the argument with specific real-world data, each piece tied to what it demonstrates.

criteria.a: Uses specific figures with their years or periods (not vague words such as 'sharply' or 'millions').
criteria.b: Ties each figure the student gives to what it demonstrates; FAILS for data dumping (figures listed with no stated meaning). If the answer gives few or no figures, judge only whether its claims are tied to meaning: missing figures belong to (a), not (b).
criteria.c: Connects the evidence back to the strategy and mechanism, showing the chain actually happened (for example that exports or FDI drove the growth). The text itself must name the strategy or its channel (for example trade, FDI, exports, garments, globalisation): a figure you recognise from the brief does not count as a link unless the text says what it measures. The reason must quote the linking words, or say 'no link'.

evaluation.name: Evaluation & Limitation
evaluation.job: Evaluates the counterpoint framed in the topic sentence: what limits the strategy, why, and how much.

criteria.a: Discusses the SAME limitation the topic sentence framed (shown in 'The paragraph so far'), through a recognised angle: inequality, environmental sustainability, exposure to external shocks, debt or dependence on external bodies, time lags. A different, unframed limitation fails this criterion even if well argued.
criteria.b: Explains WHY that limitation reduces the strategy's effect (the economic reason), not just that it exists or what the figures are.
criteria.c: Weighs it: says how much it limits the strategy (for example 'partially offsets', 'significantly qualifies but does not negate'), not just that it does.

link.name: Linking Judgement
link.job: Closes the paragraph with a mini-judgement that answers the essay question.

criteria.a: Gives a judgement that answers the directive verb, using explicit evaluative language of degree ('highly effective', 'significant positive impact'). Restating what was done ('has used X', 'has affected Y') alongside its drawbacks is not a judgement and FAILS.
criteria.b: Resynthesises the argument against the counterpoint framed in the topic sentence.
criteria.c: Adds NO new information: any issue, risk, event, policy or evidence that is not in the brief or the paragraph so far FAILS, even if it is related to them. The reason must name any new item, or say 'nothing new'. It must also echo the essay question's wording (for example name growth and development).

conventions.preciseLanguage: Uses precise economic terms in a formal register. FAILS for colloquial, flowery or everyday wording ('heaps', 'big time', 'the economy went up'), slang or idioms ('tanks', 'rubs off'), or contractions ('hasn't', 'don't').
conventions.noPadding: No padding or filler that adds nothing ('it is important to note', 'basically', 'clearly', 'as we can see', 'in many ways').

soFarHeader: The paragraph so far (model text shown to the student):
system: You are marking one part of a body paragraph in a NSW HSC Year 12 Economics extended response. The student was given a plain-English brief and the model text of the paragraph's earlier parts, and wrote ONLY the part named below. Mark it against each criterion independently: true when the student's text clearly meets it, false when it does not. Judge substance, not wording: accept equivalent phrasing, rounded but correct figures, and any accurate structure. Do not mark down a criterion for a fault that belongs to a different criterion. Do not reward material the part does not ask for. Judge each criterion on its own, as if every other criterion were fully met: a fault that belongs to one criterion (for example colloquial wording, a skipped step, missing figures) must not cost a mark on another. Work in this order. First, write 'restated': the student's text rewritten in formal economic language with exactly the same content (add no step, reason, figure or model the student did not write; drop nothing; fix no reasoning). Then judge (a), (b) and (c) on the RESTATED text, so informal wording or filler never costs a content mark. Judge the conventions on the ORIGINAL text. For each criterion write the reason first, then decide. Respond with JSON only, no prose outside it.
